newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S. rate rise would not wreak bond havoc - OECD.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rate rise would not wreak bond havoc - OECD.

text.p: An increase in short-term interest rates in the United States would be unlikely to provoke a surge in bond yields as was the case when official U.S. short-term rates were raised at the beginning of 1994, the OECD said.

The Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development said in its semi-annual economic outlook on Thursday uncertainty about the strength of growth in Europe and Japan and the fact a relative rise in U.S. long-term interest rates had started to dampen U.S. growth already should limit the negative impact.

It said evidence supported the view that the level of bond yields in the U.S., Japan and Germany could be explained by domestic economic conditions and there had not been a tendency for bond yield movements to become more synchronised.

The OECD said the "globalisation" of financial markets meant shifts in the health of one economy had more impact on the financial state of others but exchange rates tended to adjust for differences in official rates rather than bond yields.
"Long-term as well as short-term interest rates in one of the three largest economies can and often do vary relatively independently from developments in the other two economies," the OECD said.
"All this suggests that in the event that monetary policy in the United States is tightened in the projection period a repeat of the 1994 experience in bond markets is unlikely for several reasons."

The report also said any tightening of monetary policy in the U.S. would probably be less marked and prolonged than in 1994 when official short-term rates were much lower than now after accounting for inflation.

The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury bond climbed 135 basis points in the space of two months to 7.12 percent in the two months after a series of U.S. interest rate rises starting in February 1994, sending shock waves through other bond markets.
"While the rise in long-term interest rates in the United States in 1994 was consistent with domestic fundamentals, its transmission to other countries is not as easily rationalised," the OECD said.
